items.reading_summary: End of those who teach original sin and make man guilty, and who set traps for the one who spreads the truth at the 'Gate' of the Fishes (entry into Aquarius).

load_bearing.gloss: those who make a human (ʾādām) a sinner/offender by a word (or: in a case)
load_bearing.comment: Hiphil participle of ḥṭʾ, the root 'sin': literally 'who cause ʾādām to sin / declare ʾādām a sinner'. French « coupable » hides the sin-root; the object is ʾādām.

load_bearing.gloss: by a word / in a (legal) matter
load_bearing.comment: Forensic setting.

load_bearing.french: celui qui rend l’arrêt à la Porte
load_bearing.gloss: and for the one who reproves/arbitrates in the gate
load_bearing.comment: baššaʿar 'in the gate' = the city gate as law-court; a common noun. The French capital « Porte » is typographic.

load_bearing.gloss: and turn aside the righteous by emptiness (tōhû)

items.french_variance: Quotation split across TBWTT-5:10–11. « la Porte » capitalised in the quotation and re-quoted as «Porte» in 5:12. OT French presumably Dhorme; not collated.
items.analysis: Two things can be said in opposite directions. Favourable: the phrase the canon ties to original sin is, in Hebrew, built on the root ḥṭʾ 'sin' with ʾādām as object — 'those who make ʾādām a sinner by a word' — which is nearer the canon's gloss than the French « font de l'homme un coupable ». Also the same noun šaʿar stands here and in Zeph 1:10, so the 'Gate' link is lexically real. Unfavourable: the syntax and setting are forensic (false accusation in a lawsuit at the city gate, as the library note says), 'the gate' is a common noun, and nothing connects it to the Fish Gate beyond the shared word.

ellipsis.cut: 37:3b (Ezekiel's answer), 37:4–6, 37:7 'as I prophesied … bone to its bone', 37:8b 'but there was no breath in them', 37:9 (the breath called from the four winds), 37:10a 'the breath came into them'; and 37:11–14 (the vision decoded as the national restoration of Israel).
ellipsis.note: The Hebrew narrates two stages — bodies assembled but lifeless (v. 8), then rûaḥ entering (vv. 9–10) — and marks the second as the decisive one. Every mention of rûaḥ falls inside the canon's ellipses in both books, as does the passage's self-interpretation (v. 11).

items.french_variance: The reference is wrong: chapter « XXVII » for XXXVII. TBWTT-3:185 quotes the same excerpt with the correct « XXXVII ». Wording otherwise identical between the two books except punctuation: TBWTT uses « (...) » and « bruit, et voilà » / « croissait et il étendit »; ETTMTTP uses « ... » and « bruit et voilà » / « croissait, et il étendit ». The www canon_citations index silently corrects the link to chapter 37.
items.analysis: The sequence the canon matches to the re-creation machine — noise, then sinews, flesh, skin layered onto bones, then standing figures — is the Hebrew sequence, and the noise is doubly marked (qôl, raʿaš), so the hook is textual, not French. Three points run the other way. (1) Two French verbs are more 'biological' or agentive than the Hebrew: « croissait » for ʿālâ 'came up', and « il étendit » for a verb whose natural subject in v. 8 is the skin. (2) The canon's cuts remove the rûaḥ four times over: the Hebrew makes the entry of breath a separate, necessary stage and says the completed bodies were not alive without it — a feature with no counterpart in the canon's description, where the assembled body simply opens its eyes. (3) The Hebrew presents the scene as a vision and decodes it in v. 11 as the house of Israel; the canon presents it as a literal procedure. The chapter number in ETTMTTP is a misprint that the first book does not share.

items.canon_french: Vous ne mangerez point la chair avec son âme, c'es-à-dire son sang. Pour ce qui est de votre sang je le réclamerai comme vos âmes: je le réclamerai de la main de tout animal je réclamerai l'âme de l'homme de la main de l'homme, de la main d’un chacun l'âme de son frère.

reading_quotes.french: Même la Bible dit très clairement que chaque être vivant possède une «âme » et pas seulement les hommes
Donc il n'y a pas d'âme éthérée s'envolant gentiment du corps après la mort, mais il y a le code génétique qui est la personnalité de chacun.
Le mot «âme» vient du latin «anima» qui signifie «souffle de vie» ou «ce qui anime».

items.reading_summary: The Bible itself gives every living being, not only man, an 'âme', and locates it in the blood; hence no ethereal soul leaving the body — the 'soul' is the genetic code, from which the Elohim re-create the deserving.

load_bearing.french: la chair avec son âme, c'es-à-dire son sang
load_bearing.gloss: flesh with/in its nep̄eš, its blood
load_bearing.comment: nep̄eš (life, living self; library: 'throat, breath, life, living being, person') stands in apposition to 'its blood'; the French 'c'est-à-dire' makes the apposition explicit and is fair. Said here of animal flesh.

load_bearing.gloss: for/belonging to your lives
load_bearing.comment: French 'comme vos âmes' turns the lamed into an equation ('as your souls'); Hebrew is 'your blood, for your lives' (blood belonging to your life). The equation blood = âme is thus a little sharper in French than in Hebrew at this point.

load_bearing.gloss: the nep̄eš (life) of the human
load_bearing.comment: same noun used of the animal's flesh in v.4 and of the human in v.5 — the hook for 'not only men'

items.french_variance: Typographical slip «c'es-à-dire». The French wording is not that of the Job/Genesis quotations in TBWTT (no Iahvé/Élohim marker in these two verses), so the French source of this quotation cannot be identified from the dumps.
items.analysis: The textual hook is real and is Hebrew, not French: the same noun nep̄eš is predicated of animal flesh (9:4) and of the human (9:5) and is tied to blood. The Hebrew is in fact more favourable than the French word the canon has to work with: 'âme' carries the Latin/Christian sense of an immaterial soul that Raël must then argue away, whereas nep̄eš in these verses simply is the creature's life, with no separable-soul connotation (library: 'the blood IS the nefesh, the carrier of the life-force'). What the Hebrew does not supply is the step from blood-life to 'code génétique' and to re-creation; that identification is an interpretive addition. The existing library note sits at Lev 17:11 and records only that 'soul' and 'life' render the same word.
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] Latin anima = 'breath, life-principle' is the standard etymology of French âme.
[outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] Whether this French wording is Dhorme's Pléiade Genesis 9:4-5 has not been checked against the volume.

items.ref_note: first clause of the verse only
items.canon_french: Car l'âme de la chair est dans le sang.

reading_quotes.french: c'est grâce à ce code génétique que les Elohim recréent ceux qui l'ont mérité

items.reading_summary: Second proof-text for the same argument: the 'âme' of flesh is in the blood, so it is a material thing (identified with the genetic code), not an ethereal soul.

load_bearing.french: l'âme de la chair est dans le sang
load_bearing.gloss: the nep̄eš of the flesh — in the blood it is
load_bearing.comment: French literal; 'âme' = nep̄eš

ellipsis.cut: 17:11b-c: 'and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your lives; for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life' — cut silently
ellipsis.note: The cut clause does not alter the sense of the quoted clause but removes the verse's own stated purpose (atonement), leaving the anatomical statement to stand alone.

items.analysis: The clause quoted is a literal rendering and the hook (nep̄eš located in blood) is in the Hebrew. As at Gen 9, nep̄eš 'life' needs less argument than 'âme' to yield 'not an ethereal soul'. The canon quotes only the first of three clauses; the remainder — the blood is given 'upon the altar to make atonement for your lives' (ləḵappēr ʿal-nap̄šōṯêḵem) — is a cultic rationale for the blood ban, which the genetic-code reading does not address. The blood = genetic code identification is supplied by the canon.

ellipsis.cut: Matt 13:18-23 (the parable's own interpretation) is never quoted in TBWTT or LWTE
ellipsis.note: The text supplies its own decoding (seed = word; soils = hearers); the canon substitutes another without mentioning it.

items.french_variance: TBWTT-4:45: «(Certaines semences) sont tombées le long du chemin ; et les oiseaux (...) les ont dévorées» — LWTE-2:9: «De ses semences, les unes sont tombées le long du chemin et les oiseaux sont venus et les ont dévorées.» TBWTT's bracketed «(Certaines semences)» is a paraphrase of «De ses semences, les unes», and its (...) hides «sont venus et».
items.analysis: The planetary reading of sower/seed/path is supplied by the canon; the Greek is an agricultural scene of one sowing. But on one point the unquoted Greek context is closer to the canon than the verses it quotes: Matthew's own interpretation (13:19) equates the birds with ho ponēros, 'the evil one', and LWTE (unlike TBWTT-4:49, which says only «les opposants») names the birds as Satan's envoys. The canon never cites 13:18-23, where the seed is 'the word of the kingdom' and the soils are hearers — an in-text explanation that competes with the planetary one.

items.canon_french: D'autres sont tombées dans la bonne terre et ont donné du fruit, celle-ci cent, celle-là soixante, celle-là trente.

reading_quotes.french: après deux nouveaux échecs dus l'un à la trop grande proximité d'un astre dont les rayons nocifs brûlèrent leur création, et l'autre à une végétation envahissante
L'on sait que les Elohim ont créé également la vie sur deux autres planètes à cette époque, d'où l'allusion aux «trois récoltes».

items.reading_summary: Rocky ground scorched by the sun = a planet too close to a star; thorns = a planet where vegetation took over; good soil = the successful planet; the three yields (100, 60, 30) = three successful creations, Earth and two other planets.

load_bearing.french: Mais au lever du soleil elles ont été brûlées et, n'ayant pas de racines, elles ont séché.
load_bearing.original: ἡλίου δὲ ἀνατείλαντος ἐκαυματίσθη καὶ διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ῥίζαν ἐξηράνθη
load_bearing.translit: hēliou de anateilantos ekaumatisthē kai dia to mē echein rhizan exēranthē
load_bearing.gloss: when the sun rose they were scorched, and because of having no root they withered
load_bearing.comment: Greek gives the cause as lack of root/depth of soil (also 13:5 'because they had no depth of earth'); the sun is an ordinary sunrise. LWTE prints the cause clauses that TBWTT-4:46 had replaced by (...).

load_bearing.french: les épines ont monté et les ont étouffées

ellipsis.cut: LWTE quotes 13:5-9 in full; TBWTT-4:46-47 had cut 'elles ont levé aussitôt faute d'avoir épais de terre', 'et, n'ayant pas de racines, elles ont séché' and 'ont monté et'
ellipsis.note: LWTE supplies the text TBWTT elided; the restored clauses give the parable's own cause of failure for the rocky ground.

items.french_variance: TBWTT-4:46: «D’autres sont tombées parmi la rocaille, où elles n’avaient pas beaucoup de terre ; (...) mais au lever du soleil elles ont été brûlées (...)» — LWTE-2:12: «D'autres sont tombées parmi la rocaille, où elles n'avaient pas beaucoup de terre ; elles ont levé aussitôt faute d'avoir épais de terre; « Mais au lever du soleil elles ont été brûlées et, n'ayant pas de racines, elles ont séché.» TBWTT-4:47 «et les épines (...) les ont étouffées...» — LWTE-2:13 «et les épines ont monté et les ont étouffées.» 13:8-9 identical in both. Same underlying French translation, quoted in full in 1979 and with cuts in 1974.
items.analysis: Each element the canon decodes is present in the Greek (sun, thorns, good soil, three yields), and the French is literal; the planetary referents are supplied. Two points of friction with the wording: (1) the Greek states why the second batch failed — shallow soil, no root — and TBWTT cut exactly those clauses; LWTE restores them but keeps the 'too close to a star' reading; (2) the three yields are three rates of return within the fourth sowing, where the canon reads three separate successful plantings («trois récoltes» is LWTE's phrase, not the text's).

items.canon_french: C'est là qu'intervient Lucifer, nom qui étymologiquement veut dire «le porteur de lumière ». Lucifer est l'un des Elohim qui a créé la vie sur Terre et les hommes donc.

reading_quotes.french: Lucifer, le «porteur de lumière», apporte donc la lumière aux hommes en leur révélant que leurs créateurs ne sont pas des dieux mais des hommes comme eux

items.reading_summary: Lucifer is the personal name of the Eloha who led the laboratory team that told the first humans the truth (the 'serpent' group); the name means 'light-bearer' because he brought them light.

load_bearing.gloss: shining one, son of dawn (the day star)
load_bearing.comment: the only biblical source of the name: 'Lucifer' is the Vulgate's Latin common noun for hêlēl in a taunt addressed to the king of Babylon (library note); no such name occurs in Hebrew or Greek scripture

items.analysis: The Latin etymology (lux + ferre) is correct, but the name exists only in translation: it enters the tradition as the Vulgate's rendering of hêlēl in Isa 14:12, where the Hebrew is an epithet ('shining one, son of dawn') in a mocking lament over the king of Babylon, and the library note states that the identification with a fallen angel 'belongs to the reception history, not the Hebrew'. LWTE cites no verse for Lucifer and never connects him to Isa 14, although TBWTT-3:148-152 quotes Isa 14:13-17 with a different reading — the two books do not join up on this figure. A personal name 'Lucifer' for the Eden team leader is therefore a Latin-tradition label applied by the canon, with no original-language anchor.
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] lucifer is also the ordinary Latin word for the morning star (Venus).

items.canon_french: il condamne le «serpent» à ramper sur la Terre est-il écrit poétiquement

reading_quotes.french: Yahvé condamne les scientifiques qui ont désobéi à ses ordres à vivre en exil sur la Terre

items.reading_summary: The serpent condemned to crawl = Lucifer's team of scientists condemned to exile on Earth; the wording is 'poetic'.

load_bearing.gloss: on your belly you shall go
load_bearing.comment: Hebrew: locomotion on the belly, plus 'dust you shall eat' and a comparison with all cattle and wild animals; nothing about remaining on the earth/planet. French 'sur la Terre' (capital T) is the canon's paraphrase, not a quotation.

items.analysis: The exile reading hangs on the paraphrase 'ramper sur la Terre'; the Hebrew curse is 'on your belly you shall go' and classes the nāḥāš among the animals ('cursed above all cattle and every beast of the field'), with a single addressee. The canon explicitly labels the biblical wording 'poétique' here, i.e. concedes it is not being read literally. Same reading as TBWTT-2:38 (parent slice A).

items.canon_french: Or, comment dit-on «calomniateur» en grec? Tout simplement: «diabolos»!

reading_quotes.french: Satan ou l'un de ses envoyés contactait à son tour le futur prophète et lui disait beaucoup de mal des Elohim, calomniait les créateurs

items.reading_summary: The 'devil' is simply the 'slanderer': Satan or his envoys slander the Elohim to the future prophet to test his loyalty.

load_bearing.gloss: the slanderer, accuser
load_bearing.comment: etymology correct (from diaballō); library: it is the Septuagint's word for Hebrew haśśāṭān in Job 1-2

items.analysis: The etymology is right and the library glossary confirms it. The Greek gives the canon more than it uses: diabolos is the Septuagint's rendering of haśśāṭān, 'the adversary', in Job — so the Greek title links the Matthew 4 and Job figures textually, which LWTE asserts (2:48) without giving this reason. Who is slandered differs, though: in the Job scene the adversary accuses Job to YHWH, not the creators to the man.

items.canon_french: Alors Jésus fut emmené au désert par l'Esprit pour être mis à l'épreuve du diable.

reading_quotes.french: Ce qui donnerait en clair: «Alors Jésus fut emmené au désert pour être mis à l'épreuve du calomniateur. »
Or, comment dit-on «calomniateur» en grec? Tout simplement: «diabolos»!
Aussi l'on confie à Satan le soin de tester les prophètes.

items.reading_summary: The desert episode is an initiation in which Satan, one of the Elohim, is charged with testing the prophet's loyalty by slandering the creators; 'diable' is Greek diabolos, 'slanderer'.

load_bearing.gloss: to be tested / tempted
load_bearing.comment: peirazō covers both 'put to the test' and 'entice' (library note). The French the canon quotes already chooses 'test'; the Greek permits it but does not require it.

load_bearing.gloss: by the slanderer/accuser (the devil)
load_bearing.comment: 'calomniateur' is the etymological sense (library glossary diabolos-the-devil-matthew); in the Gospels it is a title, with the article

load_bearing.gloss: by the Spirit
load_bearing.comment: present in the Greek and in LWTE's quotation; dropped in LWTE's own 'en clair' paraphrase (2:34) and replaced by (...) in TBWTT-4:19

ellipsis.cut: 'par l'Esprit' (hypo tou pneumatos): cut by (...) in TBWTT-4:19, kept in LWTE-2:33's quotation, silently dropped in LWTE-2:34's 'clear' paraphrase
ellipsis.note: Removes the stated agent who leads Jesus into the desert; the canon nowhere says what 'l'Esprit' is in this verse, though TBWTT-4:19 keeps «l'Esprit de Dieu» of 3:16 in the same quotation.

items.french_variance: TBWTT-4:19: «Alors Jésus fut emmené au désert (...) pour être mis à l’épreuve du diable» — LWTE-2:33: «Alors Jésus fut emmené au désert par l'Esprit pour être mis à l'épreuve du diable. » — LWTE-2:34: «Alors Jésus fut emmené au désert pour être mis à l'épreuve du calomniateur. »
items.analysis: Both lexical hooks are Greek: diabolos does mean 'slanderer', and peirazō does mean 'test' — the Greek goes further than the quoted verse, since 4:3 calls the figure ho peirazōn, 'the tester', a participle LWTE's quotation of 4:3 omits. What the Greek does not carry is the organisational reading (Satan as an Eloha delegated to vet prophets). One ellipsis matters: the agent 'by the Spirit' is removed both times the canon restates the verse (TBWTT by (...), LWTE in its 'en clair' version), so that the only actor left is the tester.

items.canon_french: Il est écrit: l'homme ne vit pas que de pain mais de toute parole qui sort de la bouche de Dieu

reading_quotes.french: Jésus répond à Satan que le fait d'être fidèle aux Elohim est plus important que d'avoir de quoi manger

ellipsis.cut: 4:3a 'And the tester came and said to him' and the narrative link of 4:2 (forty days' fast) — skipped silently; quotation is split across LWTE-2:35 and 2:36

items.analysis: The saying is quoted accurately; the reading 'fidelity to the Elohim' substitutes a plural referent for singular theou (the Greek, quoting Deut 8:3, offers no plural). The omitted frame of 4:3 would have served the canon: ho peirazōn is literally 'the tester', the role LWTE-2:30 assigns to Satan.

items.analysis: French and Greek agree apart from the slip l'/t'. The reading changes only the referents (angels as the Elohim's messengers; 'the Lord your God' as 'his creators'), which the wording neither supports nor excludes.

items.canon_french: Va-t'en Satan, car il est écrit: Tu te prosterneras devant le Seigneur ton Dieu et le servira lui seul.

reading_quotes.french: Il faut noter au passage qu'il appelle le calomniateur par son nom, puisqu'il le nomme Satan. Et l'épreuve ayant été réussie, les «anges », les messagers des Elohim donc, viennent vers Jésus pour terminer son initiation.

load_bearing.gloss: Go away, Satan!
load_bearing.comment: anarthrous vocative: in Greek this is a personal name in direct address (library glossary satanas-satan-name-matthew) — supports 'il le nomme Satan'

load_bearing.french: des anges s'approchèrent à son service

load_bearing.original: Κύριον τὸν θεόν σου προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις

items.analysis: Two of the three lexical claims are borne out by the Greek: Satana is a name in the vocative, and angeloi are 'messengers'. This matters for the comparison with Job (E-011): the 'Satan is a personal name' claim is true of Matthew's Greek and not of Job's Hebrew, and LWTE moves from one to the other without noting the difference. 'Complete his initiation' and the plural 'Elohim' for autō monō 'him alone' are additions.

items.canon_french: Il advint un jour que les fils d'Elohim vinrent se présenter devant Yahvé et Satan vint aussi parmi eux.

reading_quotes.french: Le groupe ayant mené le combat contre ces manipulations génétiques était présidé par l'un des Elohim appelé Satan.
il indique très clairement les bons rapports, l'on pourrait même dire les rapports très fraternels qu'entretiennent Yahvé et Satan
Yahvé est hiérarchiquement audessus de Satan, mais qu'il l'autorise à exercer son activité, «d'opposant politique » en quelque sorte

items.reading_summary: Satan is the personal name of one of the Elohim, leader of the party opposed to creating humans; the Job prologue shows him among the 'sons of Elohim' in near-fraternal relations with Yahweh, his hierarchical superior, who lets him act as 'political opponent' and test Job.

load_bearing.gloss: THE adversary / the opposer (with definite article)
load_bearing.comment: Hebrew has the article throughout Job 1-2: a role title, not a proper name (library note: 'a functional role, not a proper name'). The canon's French prints bare 'Satan' as a name.

load_bearing.gloss: the sons of THE Elohim (article on Elohim)
load_bearing.comment: French drops the article; the Hebrew article marks a class ('the elohim')

load_bearing.gloss: to station themselves before YHWH
load_bearing.comment: formal presentation of court members to a sovereign (library note) — supports 'hierarchically above'

load_bearing.gloss: in their midst
load_bearing.comment: supports 'one of them / among the Elohim'

load_bearing.french: il te maudira à ta face
load_bearing.gloss: to your face he will 'bless' you
load_bearing.comment: Hebrew writes 'bless' (euphemism); French 'maudira' is the standard interpretive rendering, not the letter

items.french_variance: Divine name: TBWTT-3:250/3:252 «Iahvé» — LWTE-2:49/2:50/2:55 «Yahvé», for the same French sentences («Il advint un jour que les fils d’Elohim vinrent se présenter devant Iahvé et Satan vint aussi parmi eux»). Job 1:11: TBWTT-3:252 «A coup sûr il maudira ta face !» — LWTE-2:50 «A coup sûr il te maudira à ta face!». Job 1:12: TBWTT «et Iahvé dit à «Satan»» (name in guillemets) — LWTE «Et Yahvé dit à Satan». TBWTT cut 1:10 with (...); LWTE quotes 1:6-12 complete. The quotation is split mid-word-group across paragraphs 2:49/2:50 («Job craint | Elohim?»).
items.analysis: Split verdict, both directions. (a) The proper name: 'l'un des Elohim appelé Satan' rests on the French, which prints 'Satan' without article; the Hebrew haśśāṭān is a title with the article in every occurrence of Job 1-2, so 'named Satan' is not what Job's text says — less favourable. (b) The role: that same title means 'the adversary/opposer', which is exactly what LWTE-2:51 says he is («opposant politique»); the Hebrew common noun states the function the canon assigns, which a bare name cannot — more favourable. (c) Council setting: bənê hāʾĕlōhîm with the article, the hithpael 'present themselves' and 'in their midst' are all in the Hebrew and support a plural assembly under YHWH with the adversary as a member. 'Rapports très fraternels' is an evaluation with no lexical hook.
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] The orthography Iahvé is the Dhorme-Pléiade marker (core woh-claim-0066); 'Yahvé' in LWTE is either a normalisation or a different printing — not checked against any edition.

[outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] Whether the Pléiade text prints 'le Satan' (with article) or 'Satan' at Job 1:6 has not been checked; if it prints the article, the canon's bare 'Satan' is its own change.

items.canon_french: En tout cela Job ne pécha point et il ne proféra point de sottise à l'adresse d'Elohim.

load_bearing.gloss: YHWH gave and YHWH took
load_bearing.comment: literal; Job attributes the ruin to YHWH, not to the adversary

ellipsis.cut: Job 1:13-19 (the four disasters) skipped between the two quotations, summarised in one sentence

items.analysis: Accurate quotation. The reading only swaps the referent (Elohim as plural creators). The verse itself has Job credit both gift and loss to YHWH; the canon's summary 'Satan ruine totalement Job' follows the prologue's narrative, not Job's own words here.

items.canon_french: Il s'attache encore à sa perfection et c'est sans raison que tu m'as excité contre lui pour le ruiner.

reading_quotes.french: Mais Satan ne désarme pas, et il va faire son rapport au président du conseil des Eternels
Yahvé permet alors à Satan de ruiner la santé de Job, afin de voir s'il aimera toujours ses créateurs.

items.reading_summary: Satan 'reports' to Yahweh, president of the council of the Eternals, who allows him to ruin Job's health as a further test.

load_bearing.french: tu m'as excité contre lui pour le ruiner
load_bearing.gloss: you incited me against him to swallow him for nothing
load_bearing.comment: Hebrew sût 'incite' has YHWH say he was moved by the adversary — the test is at the adversary's initiative (library note). 'Ruiner' softens ballaʿ 'swallow up'.

load_bearing.french: Satan vint aussi parmi eux, pour se présenter devant Yahvé
load_bearing.gloss: and the adversary also came among them to present himself before YHWH
load_bearing.comment: second assembly: the adversary himself now 'presents himself' — closest textual hook for 'faire son rapport'; article again

load_bearing.gloss: only his nep̄eš (life) guard
load_bearing.comment: here the canon's French renders nep̄eš 'vie'; at Gen 9 / Lev 17 (E-003, E-004) the same noun is 'âme' and the argument is built on that word

items.french_variance: TBWTT-3:255 quotes only 2:6 «Le voici à ta discrétion ! Sauvegarde seulement sa vie !» — identical in LWTE-2:55, which adds 2:1-5. «Astu» is a typographical run-on.
items.analysis: The Hebrew of 2:1 and 2:3 carries the two things the canon needs: the adversary formally presents himself before YHWH at a periodic assembly, and YHWH states that he was incited by him — a relationship of superior and licensed opponent. These hooks are in the Hebrew at least as clearly as in the French ('excité' is weaker than sût in its juridical sense, 'ruiner' weaker than 'swallow'). The title 'président du conseil des Eternels' and the proper name 'Satan' remain additions (see E-011 for the article). Note the canon's own French uses 'vie' for nep̄eš here and 'âme' in the Genesis/Leviticus quotations.

items.canon_french: mon père qui est «dans les cieux»

reading_quotes.french: Ton véritable père est également le père de Jésus, qui est donc ton frère, et ce père tu l'as en face de toi maintenant.

items.reading_summary: The Lord's-Prayer phrase is applied literally: Yahweh, an inhabitant of another planet, is Raël's biological father (and Jesus's).

load_bearing.original: Πάτερ ἡμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
load_bearing.translit: Pater hēmōn ho en tois ouranois
load_bearing.gloss: our Father, the one in the heavens/skies
load_bearing.comment: literal; 'OUR father' in the Greek, a shared address — the canon's 'mon père' individualises it

items.analysis: The words are in the Greek as in the French (ouranoi plural = 'cieux'); the biological-paternity application is the canon's, and the prayer's possessive is plural ('our').

items.canon_french: J'ai été en esprit au jour seigneurial et j'ai entendu derrière moi une grande voix comme de trompette.

reading_quotes.french: alors qu'il essayait de communiquer télépathiquement avec nous ce qu'il appelle «être en esprit», un dimanche qui est nommé le «jour seigneurial», il a entendu une voix métallique, «comme de trompette », ce que vous connaissez bien vous qui avez l'habitude d'entendre les sons produits par des haut-parleurs électriques

items.reading_summary: 'To be in spirit' = John trying to communicate telepathically with the Elohim; 'jour seigneurial' = a Sunday; the 'great voice like a trumpet' = a metallic voice, i.e. a loudspeaker.

load_bearing.gloss: I came to be in spirit
load_bearing.comment: literal. The identical Greek phrase recurs at 4:2, where the canon reads it as being carried by a 'rayon porteur' (E-017): one phrase, two different mechanisms.

load_bearing.gloss: on the lordly (Lord's) day
load_bearing.comment: calque of the Greek adjective kyriakē; 'dimanche' is the traditional identification

load_bearing.french: une grande voix comme de trompette
load_bearing.gloss: a great (loud) voice, as of a trumpet
load_bearing.comment: Greek says megalē 'great/loud'; 'métallique' is the canon's inference from the trumpet simile

items.analysis: The French is a word-for-word calque and adds nothing the Greek lacks; the telepathy and loudspeaker readings are supplied. The trumpet comparison (hōs) describes loudness in the Greek (megalē); a metallic timbre is an inference, though a trumpet is a metal instrument. The same en pneumati receives a different technological gloss at 4:2.
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] The French wording of all LWTE Revelation quotations ('jour seigneurial', 'grosses eaux', 'bronze du Liban', 'thorax', 'esclaves', 'abri de Dieu', 'premier univers') is a very literal modern translation distinct from Segond/Crampon; it resembles Jean Grosjean's New Testament in the Bibliothèque de la Pléiade (1971), i.e. the companion volume to Dhorme's Old Testament. Not verified against that volume.

items.canon_french: et au milieu des lampes une sorte de fils d'homme revêtu jusqu'aux pieds, ceint à hauteur de poitrine d'une ceinture or,

reading_quotes.french: Il voit sept engins volants faits d'un métal doré, «sept lampes d'or», au milieu desquelles se tient un petit être, «une sorte de fils d'homme », revêtu d'une combinaison qui le moule tout entier, même les pieds, et qui porte une grosse ceinture.
le casque de son scaphandre possède deux petits projecteurs que Jean prend pour des yeux, ses pieds reposent sur d'épaisses semelles isolantes en métal jaune
Il tient dans sa main un appareil comportant sept voyants lumineux qui le relie aux sept engins volants
L'épée aiguë à deux tranchants n’est-elle en revanche qu'un détail rajouté par la suite par les copistes

items.reading_summary: Seven golden lamps = seven flying craft of golden metal; the 'son of man' = a small being in a one-piece suit covering even the feet, with a large belt; flame-eyes = two small lamps on his helmet; bronze feet = thick insulating soles of yellow metal; seven stars in his hand = a device with seven indicator lights linking him to the craft; the two-edged sword = a later copyists' addition.

load_bearing.gloss: seven golden lampstands
load_bearing.comment: lychnia is the stand that holds a lamp (lychnos), not the lamp. French 'lampes' names the luminous object; the Greek names a piece of furniture (library EN: 'lampstands').

load_bearing.gloss: clothed in a foot-length (robe)
load_bearing.comment: podērēs is a garment reaching down to the feet — a long robe. 'Revêtu jusqu'aux pieds' can be heard as 'covered right to (and including) the feet'; the Greek cannot yield a close-fitting suit enclosing the feet.

load_bearing.french: ceint à hauteur de poitrine d'une ceinture or
load_bearing.original: περιεζωσμένον πρὸς τοῖς μαστοῖς ζώνην χρυσᾶν
load_bearing.translit: periezōsmenon pros tois mastois zōnēn chrysan
load_bearing.gloss: girded at the breasts with a golden girdle/sash
load_bearing.comment: golden, worn high on the chest; 'grosse' is added

load_bearing.french: ses yeux comme une flamme de feu
load_bearing.original: οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ ὡς φλὸξ πυρός
load_bearing.translit: hoi ophthalmoi autou hōs phlox pyros
load_bearing.gloss: his eyes like a flame of fire
load_bearing.comment: literal; helmet and 'scaphandre' are not in the text

load_bearing.french: ses pieds pareils à du bronze du Liban
load_bearing.gloss: his feet like chalkolibanon
load_bearing.comment: hapax of uncertain meaning (library note: bronze alloy, bronze-frankincense, or a Semitic loan); 'bronze du Liban' is one guess. It is the feet themselves that are compared, not soles.

load_bearing.french: sept étoiles dans sa main droite
load_bearing.gloss: seven stars
load_bearing.comment: literal

load_bearing.french: une épée aiguë à deux tranchants sortant de sa bouche
load_bearing.gloss: a sharp two-edged sword proceeding
load_bearing.comment: present in the library's Greek text with no variant recorded; the canon declares it a scribal addition

ellipsis.cut: within v.12 '…' replaces 'et m'étant retourné' (kai epistrepsas); the unit stops at v.16
ellipsis.note: The internal cut is trivial. The significant omission is 1:20, handled under E-016.

items.analysis: Three of the reading's hooks lean on the French more than the Greek: 'lampes' (Greek: lampstands), 'revêtu jusqu'aux pieds' read as a body-suit enclosing the feet (Greek: a robe reaching to the feet), and 'bronze du Liban' (one conjecture for an unexplained hapax). Size ('petit'), helmet, suit, 'grosse' and the linking device are additions. Two further points are awkward: the one detail that fits no apparatus — the sword from the mouth — is removed by declaring it a copyists' gloss, although the library text records no variant; and the passage's own decoding at 1:20 ('the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches') falls in the stretch the canon skips (see E-016).
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] That no Greek manuscript omits the sword clause of Rev 1:16 is my understanding; the library note is silent on variants here.

items.canon_french: Ecris donc ce que tu as vu, ce qui est et ce qui va être après, (…)

reading_quotes.french: Nous lui avons dit que nous étions le «premier et le dernier», c'est-àdire les premiers sur la Terre, et les derniers si les hommes s'auto-détruisent
celui qui leur parlait avait connu la mort et qu'il avait été recréé, grâce au processus expliqué dans le premier message et qui nous permet de vivre éternellement à travers plusieurs corps

items.reading_summary: 'The first and the last' = the Elohim, first on Earth and last if humanity destroys itself; 'I was dead and am alive' = the speaker had died and been re-created (the cloning process); John is told to write for the time when it can be understood.

load_bearing.french: je suis le premier et le dernier
load_bearing.original: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος
load_bearing.translit: egō eimi ho prōtos kai ho eschatos
load_bearing.gloss: I am the first and the last
load_bearing.comment: singular 'I am'; the canon restates it in the plural («nous étions … les premiers … les derniers»)

load_bearing.french: J'ai été mort et voici, je suis vivant dans les âges des âges
load_bearing.original: ἐγενόμην νεκρὸς καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶν εἰμι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων
load_bearing.translit: egenomēn nekros kai idou zōn eimi eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn
load_bearing.gloss: I became dead and behold I am living unto the ages of the ages
load_bearing.comment: literal; the speaker does claim death followed by unending life — the hook for 're-created'

load_bearing.original: οἱ ἑπτὰ ἀστέρες ἄγγελοι τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησιῶν εἰσιν, καὶ αἱ λυχνίαι αἱ ἑπτὰ ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησίαι εἰσίν
load_bearing.translit: hoi hepta asteres angeloi tōn hepta ekklēsiōn eisin, kai hai lychniai hai hepta hepta ekklēsiai eisin
load_bearing.gloss: the seven stars are the angels/messengers of the seven assemblies, and the seven lampstands are seven assemblies
load_bearing.comment: this is what the canon's (…) stands in front of: v.19 is quoted complete, so the mark covers v.20

ellipsis.cut: Rev 1:20 (the mystery of the seven stars and lampstands explained as the angels of the seven churches and the seven churches); then all of chapters 2-3 (the seven letters) before the next quotation at 4:1
ellipsis.note: The omitted verse is the text's own identification of the two objects the canon has just re-identified as hardware.

items.analysis: 'Was dead and am alive for ever' is literally what the Greek says, so the re-creation reading has a real hook; 'first and last' is singular in Greek and pluralised only in the commentary. The ellipsis is the important feature: v.19 is quoted in full, so the printed (…) covers what follows — 1:20, the vision's own explanation of the seven stars and seven lampstands as the 'angels' (angeloi) of seven assemblies and the assemblies themselves. That in-text key is incompatible with stars = indicator lights and lampstands = craft, and it is the verse left out. (An ἄγγελοι/'messengers' reading of 1:20 would have been available to the canon and is not used.)

items.canon_french: Après quoi j'ai vu, et voici une porte ouverte dans le ciel. Et la première voix, comme de trompette, qui m'avait parlé m'a dit: Monte ici que je te montre ce qui doit être après.

reading_quotes.french: la porte de l'un de nos engins volants s'ouvre, et il est conduit dans l'un de ces engins par un rayon porteur, ce qui est incompréhensible pour lui, c'est pourquoi il dit «en esprit». Là, il voit quelqu'un assis dans un fauteuil, et autour de lui sur d'autres trônes, d'autres personnages sont assis, vingtquatre en tout.
Ce personnage, c'était moi Yahvé et j'étais entouré de vingt-quatre autres éternels représentant le conseil des Eternels gouvernant notre Planète.

items.reading_summary: 'A door open in the sky' = the door of a craft; 'in spirit' = lifted by a carrier beam; the throne = an armchair in which Yahweh sits, with twenty-four other Eternals = the governing council.

load_bearing.french: une porte ouverte dans le ciel
load_bearing.gloss: a door standing opened in the heaven/sky
load_bearing.comment: literal

load_bearing.gloss: come up here
load_bearing.comment: literal — a physical ascent is commanded

load_bearing.gloss: at once I came to be in spirit
load_bearing.comment: same phrase as 1:10, there read as attempted telepathy, here as transport by beam

load_bearing.french: un trône était dans le ciel et quelqu'un assis sur le trône
load_bearing.original: θρόνος ἔκειτο ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν θρόνον καθήμενος
load_bearing.translit: thronos ekeito en tō ouranō, kai epi ton thronon kathēmenos
load_bearing.gloss: a throne was set in the heaven, and on the throne one seated
load_bearing.comment: literal

load_bearing.original: θρόνους εἴκοσι τέσσαρες, καὶ ἐπὶ τοὺς θρόνους εἴκοσι τέσσαρας πρεσβυτέρους καθημένους
load_bearing.translit: thronous eikosi tessares, kai epi tous thronous eikosi tessaras presbyterous kathēmenous
load_bearing.gloss: twenty-four thrones, and on the thrones twenty-four elders seated
load_bearing.comment: 4:4 is paraphrased, not quoted; presbyteroi 'elders' — a deliberative body of seniors is a natural sense of the Greek word

ellipsis.cut: chapters 2-3 skipped before; 4:3-11 (rainbow, lightning, seven lamps of fire 'which are the seven spirits of God', sea of glass, four living creatures, the hymn) not quoted — only the twenty-four are paraphrased; chapter 5 (scroll, Lamb) omitted entirely before 6:2
ellipsis.note: The Lamb who opens the seals (5:6-6:1) disappears; in the canon the seals are simply 'opened'.

items.analysis: All the objects are in the Greek as in the French: an opened door in the sky, a command to come up, a seated figure on a throne, twenty-four seated presbyteroi ('elders' — the canon says 'éternels … conseil', and a council of elders is what the word describes). Craft, beam and armchair are identifications. Internal inconsistency: en pneumati is glossed as telepathy at 1:10 and as a carrier beam here.

items.canon_french: Et j'ai vu, et voici un cheval blanc et celui qui était dessus avait un arc. On lui a donné une couronne et il est sorti vainqueur et pour vaincre.

reading_quotes.french: Cela concerne le premier des sept sceaux, ou encore des sept chapitres de l'histoire de l'humanité. Il s'agit en fait du christianisme qui triomphe sur la terre et qui permet à l'Ancien Testament d'être connu de tous.

items.reading_summary: Seven seals = seven chapters of human history; the white horse = Christianity triumphing and spreading the Old Testament.

load_bearing.french: il est sorti vainqueur et pour vaincre
load_bearing.gloss: he went out conquering and in order to conquer
load_bearing.comment: literal

items.analysis: A historical-allegorical reading with no technological content; the wording is neutral between the readings the library note lists (Christ, Antichrist, conquest in general, Parthian archers), and the canon's choice sits near the first.

items.canon_french: Un autre cheval est sorti, rouge. Celui qui était dessus, on lui a donné d'ôter la paix de la terre, que les gens s'entr'égorgent et on lui a donné un grand sabre.

reading_quotes.french: Ce cheval rouge représente les guerres de religions, et les guerres en général

items.reading_summary: Red horse = wars of religion and wars in general, a main brake on human population growth.

load_bearing.gloss: so that they slaughter one another
load_bearing.comment: literal ('égorger' = sphazō)

items.analysis: War is what the Greek describes (peace taken from the earth, mutual slaughter, a great sword); 'of religion' is added.

items.canon_french: Et j'ai entendu comme une voix au milieu des quatre animaux crier: Un denier la mesure de blé ! un denier les trois mesures d'orge! et l'huile et le vin ne les gâche pas !

reading_quotes.french: Ce cheval noir, c'est la famine

items.reading_summary: Black horse = famine.

load_bearing.french: Un denier la mesure de blé
load_bearing.gloss: a choinix of wheat for a denarius
load_bearing.comment: literal; scarcity pricing

ellipsis.cut: 6:5a ('when he opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature say: Come') replaced by '...'

items.analysis: The famine reading is the plain sense of the balance and the prices and is the ordinary reading of the passage.

items.ref_note: first half of 6:8 only
items.canon_french: Et j'ai vu, et voici un cheval vert et celui qui était dessus s'appelait La Peste. Et l'Hadès le suivait.

reading_quotes.french: Le cheval vert, ce sont les grandes épidémies, la peste et bien d'autres qui décimeront aussi l'humanité.

items.reading_summary: Green horse = the great epidemics, plague and others.

load_bearing.gloss: his name (was) Death
load_bearing.comment: the rider's name in Greek is 'Death'. The French 'La Peste' takes thanatos in its Septuagintal sense 'pestilence' — the sense the library EN gives the same word later in this verse (en thanatō, 'with pestilence') but not for the name.

load_bearing.gloss: a green / pale-green horse
load_bearing.comment: 'vert' is the basic sense of chlōros; more literal than the usual 'pale'

ellipsis.cut: 6:8b: 'and authority was given to them over a quarter of the earth, to kill with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by the wild beasts of the earth' — cut silently
ellipsis.note: The cut clause shows the rider's remit is wider than disease.

items.analysis: The reading 'epidemics' is read straight off the French name 'La Peste'. The Greek rider is 'Death', with Hades following; and the half of the verse the canon cuts gives the pair authority to kill 'with sword and with famine and with pestilence and by the wild beasts' — four means, of which pestilence is one. So the Greek makes the fourth horse death in general (summing up the previous riders), where the French permits a clean sequence war / famine / plague.
outside_knowledge: [outside knowledge — unverified, needs source] That thanatos renders Hebrew deḇer 'pestilence' in the Septuagint, which is why some translations give 'Peste/Pestilence' here.

items.canon_french: Quand il a ouvert le cinquième sceau, j'ai vu sous l'autel les âmes de ceux qui ont été égorgés à cause de la parole de Dieu et à cause du témoignage qu'ils portaient.

reading_quotes.french: Cette scène représente ce qui s'est produit lorsque les grands prophètes qui vivaient éternellement en notre compagnie sur notre planète nous ont demandé de permettre aux hommes ayant agi positivement d'être recréés avant que le jugement final n'ait eu lieu

items.reading_summary: The scene = the great prophets living on the Elohim's planet asking that deserving humans be re-created before the final judgment; a few thousand were then re-created at once rather than held as genetic codes.

load_bearing.french: les âmes de ceux qui ont été égorgés
load_bearing.gloss: the souls/lives of those who had been slaughtered
load_bearing.comment: the canon quotes 'âmes' seen 'under the altar' after death without comment, although LWTE-1:69 denies any soul surviving death

load_bearing.gloss: (how long until) you avenge our blood
load_bearing.comment: the speakers are the slain themselves and what they ask for is judgment and vengeance

load_bearing.french: On leur a donné à chacun un vêtement blanc et on leur a dit de reposer encore un peu
load_bearing.original: ἐδόθη αὐτοῖς ἑκάστῳ στολὴ λευκή, καὶ ἐρρέθη αὐτοῖς ἵνα ἀναπαύσωνται ἔτι χρόνον μικρόν
load_bearing.translit: edothē autois hekastō stolē leukē, kai errethē autois hina anapausōntai eti chronon mikron
load_bearing.gloss: a white robe was given to each, and they were told to rest yet a little time
load_bearing.comment: the answer is to wait, until more are killed

items.analysis: French and Greek agree; the reading fits neither closely. In the text the petitioners are the martyrs, the petition is for vengeance, and the reply is 'rest a little longer'; in the canon the petitioners are living prophets, the petition is for early re-creation of others, and the reply is consent. The only shared elements are a petition and a gift (white robe ~ new body). The passage also sits uneasily with LWTE-1:69: psychai of the dead, seen and speaking, are quoted here without the 'no soul' gloss.

items.canon_french: le ciel s'est retiré comme un livre qu'on roule et toute montagne ou île ont été bougées de leur lieu.

reading_quotes.french: Ce sixième sceau représente le danger final pour l'humanité, le plus grand danger, celui qui peut la détruire totalement, la guerre atomique.

Le «ciel qui se retire» ce sont les nuages qui sont chassés brutalement par la colonne d'air chaud qui se dégage. Quant aux hommes qui se cachent dans les roches des montagnes, c'est la ruée vers les abris antiatomiques.

items.reading_summary: Sixth seal = atomic war: 'great shaking' = the explosion; black sun and dark moon = the mushroom cloud and dust; 'sky withdrawing' = clouds driven off by the column of hot air; people hiding in rocks = the rush to fallout shelters.

load_bearing.gloss: a great shaking/earthquake occurred
load_bearing.comment: seismos is literally 'a shaking'; the French 'secousse' keeps that generality where most versions say 'earthquake'

load_bearing.french: le ciel s'est retiré comme un livre qu'on roule
load_bearing.original: ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον
load_bearing.translit: ho ouranos apechōristhē hōs biblion helissomenon
load_bearing.gloss: the sky was parted/withdrawn like a scroll being rolled up
load_bearing.comment: literal

load_bearing.french: se sont cachés dans les antres et dans les roches des montagnes
load_bearing.original: ἔκρυψαν ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τῶν ὀρέων
load_bearing.translit: ekrypsan heautous eis ta spēlaia kai eis tas petras tōn oreōn
load_bearing.gloss: hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains
load_bearing.comment: literal

load_bearing.original: κρύψατε ἡμᾶς ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ καθημένου ἐπὶ τοῦ θρόνου καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς τοῦ ἀρνίου
load_bearing.translit: krypsate hēmas apo prosōpou tou kathēmenou epi tou thronou kai apo tēs orgēs tou arniou
load_bearing.gloss: hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb
load_bearing.comment: the next verse, not quoted, states what they hide from

ellipsis.cut: 6:16-17 (the plea to mountains and rocks: 'hide us from the face of the one seated on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come')
ellipsis.note: Supplies an explicit cause for the hiding that differs from the canon's.

items.analysis: Every image the canon maps is in the Greek as in the French (shaking, darkened sun, blood-coloured moon, sky rolling back, flight to caves), and 'secousse' is if anything truer to seismos than 'tremblement de terre'. The mapping itself is supplied; the falling stars (6:13) get no gloss. The quotation stops one verse short of the text's own statement of what the people are hiding from — 'the face of the one seated on the throne and the wrath of the Lamb' (6:16-17). In the canon's own scheme the one on the throne is Yahweh (E-017), so the unquoted verse would make the hiding a flight from him, not from a blast.

items.canon_french: Ne nuisez pas à la terre ni à la mer ni aux arbres tant que nous n'aurons pas scellé au front les esclaves de notre Dieu.

reading_quotes.french: Ceux qui sont scellés au front, ce sont ceux qui ont fait effectuer la transmission de leur plan cellulaire, par contact manuel entre notre prophète et l'os frontal qui contient le code génétique le plus pur et le plus fidèle. Le total de ceux qui seront «scellés au front» sera d'à peu près cent quarante-quatre mille

items.reading_summary: Sealed on the forehead = those whose 'cellular plan' has been transmitted by the prophet's hand on the frontal bone; about 144,000 in all; the cataclysm is delayed until that number is reached.

load_bearing.original: σφραγίσωμεν τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἐπὶ τῶν μετώπων αὐτῶν
load_bearing.translit: sphragisōmen tous doulous tou theou hēmōn epi tōn metōpōn autōn
load_bearing.gloss: (until) we seal the slaves of our God on their foreheads
load_bearing.comment: forehead and sealing are in the Greek; plural 'foreheads'

load_bearing.gloss: the slaves of our God
load_bearing.comment: French 'esclaves' is the literal sense of doulos

load_bearing.french: d'à peu près cent quarante-quatre mille
load_bearing.original: ἑκατὸν τεσσεράκοντα τέσσαρες χιλιάδες, ἐσφραγισμένοι ἐκ πάσης φυλῆς υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ
load_bearing.translit: hekaton tesserakonta tessares chiliades, esphragismenoi ek pasēs phylēs huiōn Israēl
load_bearing.gloss: a hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed out of every tribe of the sons of Israel
load_bearing.comment: 7:4 is alluded to, not quoted: the Greek number is exact and is drawn from the tribes of Israel (12 × 12,000 in vv.5-8); the canon makes it approximate and universal

ellipsis.cut: 7:4-8 (the number and its tribal breakdown) and 7:9-17; then 8:1-6 (silence, censer) before 8:7
ellipsis.note: The source of the 144,000 and its restriction to the tribes of Israel is not shown to the reader.

items.analysis: The anatomical hook — a mark applied to the forehead that protects from the coming harm — is in the Greek exactly as in the French. The mechanism (frontal bone, genetic code, manual contact) is added. The number is taken from the unquoted v.4, where it is exact and explicitly Israelite by tribe; 'à peu près' and the extension to all deserving humans depart from that wording.

items.ref_note: 8:7a ('the first sounded') paraphrased in the lead-in
items.canon_french: ça été de la grêle et du feu mêlés de sang et jetés sur la terre, et le tiers de la terre a été brûlé, le tiers des arbres ont brûlé, toute herbe verte a brûlé.

reading_quotes.french: Le tiers de la terre est brûlé par la radioactivité, les arbres et l'herbe verte ne poussent plus.

items.reading_summary: First trumpet of the seventh seal = a third of the earth burned by radioactivity; trees and grass no longer grow.

load_bearing.french: le tiers de la terre a été brûlé
load_bearing.gloss: a third of the earth was burned up
load_bearing.comment: literal; this clause is in the critical Greek text and the canon's French but absent from the KJV used by the canon's English edition (library note)

load_bearing.french: de la grêle et du feu mêlés de sang et jetés sur la terre
load_bearing.original: χάλαζα καὶ πῦρ μεμιγμένα ἐν αἵματι, καὶ ἐβλήθη εἰς τὴν γῆν
load_bearing.translit: chalaza kai pyr memigmena en haimati, kai eblēthē eis tēn gēn
